problem: Sewing efficiency had held between 43% and 47% for three consecutive years (FY19-20 47%, FY20-21 45%, FY21-22 43%) against a 65% requirement. Three-month record base 40%; six-day observation study 51%. Line OEE spread 17% to 73% across the floor on the same machines and the same operators, which located the gap in the operating system rather than the asset base. Four causes carried the gap. First, material staging: line availability was 94% but no-loading was 42% of all downtime, so lines with no cut panels were the largest single stoppage. Second, line balance: manpower was deployed against the operation bulletin rather than the limiting station, with Grade A operators short by 65 against the plan, a total shortfall of 37 to 40 operators, and 8% absence with no multi-skill cover pool. Third, changeover: a single changeover on Line-6 ran 4.8 hours of which 290 minutes was non-value work, led by loading delay at 110 minutes. Fourth, defects: 8.1% average over six months with uncut thread alone at 20% of occurrences, and rework returning to the same station and stopping it twice. Order execution mapping across eight December-21 orders showed sewing running 26 days against a 22-day standard, and file receipt running 29 days beyond standard. The file receipt gap is an order-side item upstream of the plant and was excluded from scope.
levers: One governing KPI. Three days of cut material available at every line before the shift started, tracked daily, with cutting, planning, quality and HR reorganised to serve it. (1) Material to the line: four planning rules counted back from the loading date — order into the fortnightly rolling plan at 21 days; fabric, trims and file confirmed at 8 days; cutting plan issued table by table with the loading quantity named at 2 days; panels checked, staged in the supermarket and matched to the line at 1 day. Installed with a three-day WIP tracker, supermarket tracking, 100% panel check in cutting before release to sewing, a deviation note requiring approval before any unplanned change, table-wise hourly targets and run-hour allocation in cutting, and a dedicated cutting owner reporting into the daily review. (2) Line balance at the limiting station: a four-move sequence applied in order — match the highest cycle time to the second highest where the difference is under two seconds; upskill the operator to the standard cycle time; recheck which station now limits the line; only then add an operator, at the lowest grade the station allows. Deployment planned one day ahead line by line and station by station, with a multi-skill pool sized to cover 8% absence. (3) Changeover and defects: revised changeover process with a changeover tracker and a deployed changeover team, offline pre-setting of critical machines, loading quantity confirmed two days ahead, the critical operator named before batch setting, a downtime tracker installed, and root cause reviews on the top defects with named owners and dated actions. (4) MCS backbone, five layers, each with plan, control, report and action log: hourly short interval control at the line and the cutting table; daily review in sewing and in cutting chaired by the section head; plant head daily review on tomorrow's material; weekly planning and coordination meeting chaired by the Senior VP; fortnightly steering committee. Nineteen system elements, each with a named client owner and a named improvement team member, scored weekly on both compliance and use. (5) Operator supply: village recruitment moved from Sunday-only to daily, operator skill mapped down to activity level rather than grade, upskilling directed at the stations that limit lines, and exit calls made to understand separations.
impact: Sewing efficiency 40% base to 52% across all lines and 55% on lines holding three days of cut material, by August 2022. Against the three-year base this is a gain of 12 points on the whole floor with no new machine and no new shift. Lines holding three days of cut material 8 to 22 in five weeks (+175%), and 17 of 20 in August. Lines running above 50% efficiency 5 to 14 over the same five weeks. Efficiency improved 23% over base by week 16 and 36% in the five weeks after material tracking started. The served-versus-unserved split held every week it was measured: 45% against 38% in the week of 3 June, 55% against a 52% plant average in August. System compliance reached 100% on 17 of the 19 elements by week 23, from an April spread of 50% to 79%. Line-11 output 739 to 800 pieces per day from three seconds of cycle time across two stations. Changeover opportunity of 4.8 hours to 1.5 hours identified and acted on, with 290 minutes of non-value work isolated. Recruitment reached 92 villages and 443 graded prospects in nine weeks, with 74 operators onboarded by end April. Forward bridge at handover: seven levers carrying the remaining 13 points from 52% to the 65% target, each with a dashboard, a named owner and a weekly number. No rupee or dollar EBITDA figure is certified in the programme record for this engagement. Do not quote one. Lead with the efficiency and system numbers, which are measured.
fit: Any labour-intensive assembly operation where output is set by material reaching the line rather than by machine capacity: garments, footwear, leather goods, wiring harness, light electrical assembly. Strongest case in the library for two specific moves. First, the single-KPI operating model, where one measurable condition is chosen and the whole plant is organised around serving it daily. Second, MCS handover, where every routine is scored on compliance and on use, and passed to a client team that runs it after the programme ends. Also the right case for an exporter whose buyers drive high changeover frequency, and for any plant where a wide line-to-line spread on identical assets is visible in the data. Pitch angle: lines in the same shed, on the same machines, with the same operators, ran between 17% and 73%. The spread is the opportunity, and it is not a machine problem.

label: Extruded Snacks / FMCG (CRAX brand)
problem: Output was set by the plant's ability to hold a daily rate, not by installed capacity. The daily average moved from about 19,200 cases in November 2025 to 22,267 in January 2026, fell to 16,809 in March, and recovered to 19,830 in April. Across the whole period only five days reached 24,000 cases. Line-1 carried 58% of the total gap at 70% target attainment, driven by extruder performance falling from 71% to 49%. Three clusters carried the March fall: floor and space work shutdowns, extruder performance loss on L1 and L3, and weigher and startup losses. Manpower shortage was the single largest stoppage driver at 67,558 minutes across March and April, ahead of HMI hang and network errors. Finished goods and floor space stoppage was the largest flow constraint on the packing lines. Daily management existed as reporting rather than as a closed loop, so the same issues returned week after week without an owner or a due date.
levers: (1) Daily operating rhythm, installed as the 24K Dream Run: manpower sign-off at 06:30 against the day's plan; two-hourly production status published to the plant group; continuous extruder speed monitoring with alert thresholds set for Line-1; a five-minute line stoppage trigger that escalates before the loss compounds. (2) Three coordination streams run in parallel: planning and dispatch on a two-day rolling plan with daily truck planning; manpower with a new seasonal contractor enrolled to close the shortage; maintenance with PM compliance driven from 20% to 50%. (3) Twenty-eight management systems built across production, maintenance, dispatch, planning, HR, 5S and engineering stores. Every system is closed loop: capture, review, action, escalate, review again. Each carries a named client owner and a single operational objective, and the systems group into three impact themes, run-rate, reliability and flow. (4) Governance in three layers, each with plan, control, report and action log: daily review, fortnightly steering committee, monthly review. (5) Shopfloor condition and 5S: 48 initiatives finalised with the team at ₹1.4 Cr, of which ₹0.9 Cr CapEx and ₹0.4 Cr R&M, led by PU floor coating at ₹48 lakh, gangway and jogging track marking, drainage in the extruder and seasoning areas, warehouse lighting and roof ventilation. Zone-wise 1S and 2S audit scoring installed with a monthly best and worst zone published. (6) A weekly continual improvement tracker carrying the top issues out of each steering committee with owner, due date and case-per-day impact.
impact: Throughput +19% across the engagement, agreed with the client as the programme headline at handover. Twenty-eight management systems built, 21 live at handover and 7 on a defined completion path. Finished goods and space stoppage reduced 96%, and held below 40 hours for two consecutive months, which was the sustenance test the client set. PM compliance 20% to 50%. Post-handover monitoring to August 2026 records 105% of the Phase-1 throughput target and 95% of the Phase-2 throughput target. Basis note for internal use: the 19% is the pre-programme run-rate against the current run-rate as agreed with the client. Measured on full-target days from December to April the lift is +2.4%. State the basis if a prospect asks. Invoicing did not rise during the engagement because the plant was demand-constrained, not capacity-constrained, so this case proves capacity release and system durability, not revenue growth. No EBITDA figure is certified in the programme record for this engagement. Do not quote one. Lead with throughput, systems handed over, and sustenance held after exit.
fit: Any packaged food or FMCG plant whose output swings day to day and which cannot hold a daily target on lines it already owns: snacks, biscuits, confectionery, ready-to-eat, beverage packing. Strongest case in the library for the durability argument, where the board's real question is not whether output can be lifted but whether the lift survives the consultant leaving. Use the 28 closed-loop systems, the named owners and the two-month sustenance evidence as the answer. Pairs with F4 the client for FMCG conversion cost and digital governance, and with M17 the client for multi-SKU packing lines. Pitch angle: five lines in one plant, the same product, the same shift pattern, and only five days in six months touched the target. The gap sat in the daily operating system, not in the assets. Also the right case for a promoter or board that wants systems handed over with named owners rather than a report at exit.

label: Transmission Towers, Steel Fabrication and Galvanizing
sector: Transmission Towers, Steel Fabrication and Galvanizing
problem: Board objective was 9,500 MT a month through both fabrication and galvanizing, against a fabrication baseline of 4,230 MT a month averaged over April to December 2025, about 141 MT a day. Diagnosis put the realisable potential from the existing asset base at 8,052 MT a month and decomposed the 3,822 MT gap into four losses: shopfloor productivity 1,532 MT, manpower unavailability 698 MT, machine breakdown 462 MT and raw material supply 230 MT, with 900 MT to come from full use of the new SCM machines. A machine time study found that of 435 available minutes only 310 were run time, with changeover at 37 minutes, shift changeover 25, breakdown 25, inspection 12 and the balance across operator away, material handling and lunch delay. Galvanizing ran at 95 dips a day and dips per shift swung between 16 and 41 against an average of 31, held down by a worn and misaligned crane rail track and by jams in the downstream area. Once fabrication started lifting, galvanizing became the binding constraint and fell to 70 dips a day in March and 79 in April, 17% below its own base, so the fabrication gain could not convert into dispatch.
levers: (1) Raw material supply: 12,000 MT of steel sorted by profile, length and type into 72 mapped bins, material relayout to spread load across the cranes, a two-bin kanban at every machine with a light based call system, and two joint line walks a shift by the raw material and fabrication supervisors to set the next four hours of supply. (2) Maintenance and reliability: checklist condition monitoring with 18 critical check points every 10 days, daily cleaning, lubrication and inspection by the operator, machine criticality defined and PM frequency moved from quarterly to monthly, 137 critical spares brought under a stores min-max model, a structured weekly RCA session on the last seven days of breakdowns, and a manager model machine system putting four CNC groups under four named managers. (3) Manpower availability: short-term advance leave planning giving two-day forward visibility on attendance, attendance tracked against commitment, scoring and counselling for repeat absence, and a daily review meeting running at 95% plus adherence with deviations logged. (4) Shopfloor productivity: Short Interval Control installed to catch losses inside the shift, a running shift handover to cut changeover at the shift break, SMED on high-frequency changeovers, changeover and quality check tracking per machine per shift feeding the daily SIC review, and a Gemba Passport with four teams, a daily 15 minute Gemba meeting, all eight losses plus absenteeism tracked in ECU and recognition tied to KPI closure. (5) Planning: the ECU methodology built as the common planning unit, measurement started and the planning process handed to the operations team, with SAP integration of hole counts in the BOM for sustained use and 12,000 drawings processed manually and with an AI agent. (6) Galvanizing: fortnightly crane preventive maintenance, daily crane condition monitoring, furnace burner PM with air and fuel mix optimisation, daily irritant identification and resolution, shift and rack wise dipping plans to manage downstream load, standardised unloading by station and material category, crane rail track replacement as the critical path capex, shed length extension for more racks, and a two-crane dedicated dipping proof of concept to cut cycle time from 13.5 minutes to 10. (7) Mechanisation defined in three areas: rack loading and unloading, vertical storage in finished and semi-finished goods, and the filing process, the last worth up to 18 operators a shift. (8) Inventory rebuilt to hold 1.75 to 2.0 times factory throughput so that material starvation stops being a production loss.
impact: Fabrication 141 MT a day at baseline to 275 MT a day, a 95% increase, which is above the 268 MT a day the 8,052 MT monthly potential implies, so the full identified potential from the existing asset base has been reached. Galvanizing 95 dips a day at baseline, down to 79 in April on crane rail track failure, now 124 dips a day, 31% above base and 57% above the April low, past the 115 dip Stage-1 target and moving toward the 159 dip full potential. Total identified losses down 43% from baseline. Manpower unavailability loss 698 MT at base to 231 MT in January to 111 MT in April, an 84% reduction. Raw material supply loss 329 MT in January, 888 MT at the March peak, 214 MT in April, a 35% cut against January. Shopfloor productivity loss 1,532 MT at base to 1,075 MT. Inside the shift, shift changeover loss 25 minutes to 5, inspection 12 to 4, material loading 9 to 2, material unloading and lunch delay to zero. Adoption position at the last review, and the reason the extension is being sought: ECU is not yet the working language at central planning, the two-crane dipping process can hold 138 to 140 normalised dips a day but the team is targeting 132, and the daily review, weekly OPEX and weekly RCA platforms are still read as consultant-led, with only the COO's fortnightly review settled as a habit. Breakdown loss is the one line that has not moved, 462 MT at base against 502 MT in April. No EBITDA figure is certified in the programme record. Do not quote one. Lead with the throughput, dip rate and loss reduction numbers, which are measured.
fit: Any plant where a fabrication or forming process feeds a single shared finishing asset: transmission and telecom towers, lattice structures, structural steel, galvanized fabrication, and any hot dip galvanizing or coating line serving several upstream units. Strongest case in the library for the constraint-shift argument. Lifting the first process 95% did not lift dispatch, because the finishing process became the binding constraint and had to be recovered separately. Use it with any client whose plan is to raise output in one area without reading what sits downstream of it. Also the right case for a listed company that has bought capacity ahead of demand and now has to convert paid-for assets into output, and for any board that wants the loss decomposition shown in tonnes rather than percentages. Pairs with M4 the client for heavy fabrication throughput. Pitch angle: the potential was not in new machines. It was 3,822 MT a month sitting in four named losses, and 435 available minutes a machine of which only 310 were run time.

label: Railway Division, Rail Line Doubling EPC
sector: Railway Division, Rail Line Doubling EPC
problem: A section that should have completed in 153 days took 452 days, a 195% overrun. The overrun decomposed into planning failures and site productivity failures rather than into any external cause. On planning: backward scheduling was not done properly, so delay was built into the plan before work started; critical and non-critical paths were not defined; no resource or crew estimate existed; the plan was never converted into daily targets or short interval schedules; and interviews showed a wide gap between what planning held and what execution understood, so the plan had no role in the actual work. On site productivity: earth cutting ran one day of work in 2.5 days, rock drilling one day in two, slush removal and blanketing one day in eight, and track linking one day in three. Site productivity measured 40%, 56% and 68% at different stages, with 26% of the loss from no crew and 18% from formation not ready. Excavators lost about a third of productive time to rework, sat idle waiting for vehicles while both supervisors watched the excavator, and HYVAs were poorly allocated all day. On the supply streams: 54 days on average to make murram available for blanketing, 33 days to identify a source at a 50% hit rate, 18 days for government approval, no pug mill and a low blending rate; 32 days on average to make ballast available for permanent way, with crusher uptime at 50% and only 6 net production hours a day; 24 days to line up a contractor and 23 days for purchase order approval, with work in some cases starting before a PO existed, which delayed contractor payment and stopped work at site. Rework ran at 41% of RFIs, driven by poor murram quality across quarries and untagged blending ratios. Seven of the 35 parts needed for track linking were critical on availability. Attrition at key execution positions added induction time because handover was informal.
levers: Designed at diagnosis, presented as the route to the 50% lead time reduction. (1) Critical chain path method as the planning backbone: critical and non-critical paths defined, backward scheduling built properly from the finish date, site conditions used to correct productivity norms, resources and crews estimated against the plan, and locations and approach roads identified before work starts. (2) Window plans for the non-critical streams that decide the critical path anyway: murram, ballast and bridges, each with a named owner. (3) Management control system in tiers: the plan converted into daily targets, short interval control on site, formal daily review meetings, weekly cross-functional reviews as a problem-solving platform rather than a status report, and progress tracking on plan versus actual for time rather than volume alone. (4) Quality and rework control: RFT and turnaround delays measured, blending ratio tagged for every murram lot with a lab test after blending, and root cause analysis on repeat problems instead of on one-off events. (5) Sourcing run as a process: murram sourcing managed like a sales pipeline given its low hit rate, ballast sourcing given defined ownership at execution level, and PO release treated as seriously as PO approval, with a regular PO status review across all stakeholders. (6) Behavioural conditions named as prerequisites: timeline targets made part of performance management, line walks made routine, and local issues categorised and pre-empted rather than generalised.
impact: Diagnosis stage. Opportunity quantified as a reduction of execution lead time by up to 50%, against the measured 195% overrun on the reference section. The measured findings that carry the case are the activity ratios, one day of work taking 2.5, 2, 8 and 3 days across earth cutting, rock drilling, blanketing and track linking, the 41% rework rate on RFIs, the 54 and 32 day sourcing lead times for murram and ballast, and the 24 and 23 day contractor and PO lead times. No implementation result, and no rupee figure, is certified in this record. Do not present it as a delivered case until the implementation numbers are added.
fit: Any EPC or site-execution business where the schedule slips and nobody can say which part of the chain caused it: rail, transmission and distribution, roads, pipelines, substations, tower erection and stringing. Use it as the site-side counterpart to the plant-side cases. The strongest analytical move is the decomposition of a single section from 153 planned days to 452 actual days, and the finding that the delay was inside planning and site control rather than in the local conditions everyone blamed. The line that lands with an EPC audience: the plan remained a plan, and had no role in the actual execution. Pairs directly with M26 the client for a T&D client, where the plant gain has to convert through site erection and certification. Note the date. This is a 2014 diagnosis, so lead with the method and the decomposition rather than with recency.

label: Iron Castings Foundry (Units 1 and 2)
problem: All three lines run below 50% OEE and the loss is upstream, not on the line. DF-90 Unit 2 at 38.6% (availability 70.9%, efficiency 62.9%, mould quality 86.6%) producing 458 of a possible 1,202 moulds a day at the 72 second standard. DF-70 at 47.8% (80.7%, 63.5%, 93.3%) producing 974 of 2,083 at 41.5 seconds. DF-90 Unit 1 at 36.8% (83.0%, 47.8%, 92.9%) producing 464 of 1,200. Availability loss runs 419, 267 and 244 minutes a day with 99.8% of it unplanned, and twelve machines carry about 92% of line breakdown time. Efficiency loss runs 377, 424 and 622 minutes a day, with metal delay, pouring stop and core handling carrying 48% to 58% of it. Cycle time studies showed the lines are not slow but stop hard: DF-90 Unit 2 held 49.8% of the 67 second standard with 22 stoppages in 207 cycles carrying 76% of lost time, DF-90 Unit 1 held 54.2% of standard with 28 stoppages in 208 cycles carrying 61%, DF-70 held 45.7% of standard with 11 stoppages in 156 cycles carrying 71%. Melting was the first upstream constraint: Unit 1 tap to tap ran 103.5 minutes against a 49.0 minute standard, a 111% overrun, with the sampling loop alone at 35.0 minutes against 5.0, and power off for 46% of every cycle; Unit 2 Furnace 4 ran 75.0 minutes against 51.5. First time right chemistry stood at 90.5%, with 611 of 6,431 heats failing, 69% of failures on carbon and 29% on silicon. Ground leakage stoppages cost 80.2 hours in seven months across 62 events, 20% of all downtime days, with contamination behind 69% of them, and lining life averaged 274 heats against the 322 the same furnaces deliver when a campaign runs to full life, with only 58% of campaigns doing so. Sand plant breakdowns stopped DF-90 for 101 minutes and DF-70 for 55 minutes a day, 70% to 85% of it from the return sand group and the sand mixer. Core unavailability stopped the DF-90 line for 43 minutes a day, with cores present at the line for only 5 to 12 minutes against 45 to 50 minutes of available space, and core rejection ran 12.1% on cold box against 7.1% on airset with handling and making defects behind 85.5% of it. Quality loss ran 66.6 bad moulds a production day, 38.0 from five categories, and box level analysis showed 35 boxes carrying 149 of 242 bad moulds on DF-90, so the fault sat with the box and not only with the pattern. Around the plant: the scrap yard took in 1,368 MT more than it issued over 128 days with dead stock occupying 32% to 40% of capacity, the furnace and ladle crane fleet ran at 62% utilisation with 248 recoverable idle minutes, contract manpower was fulfilled at 83.5% of sanctioned strength leaving 112 heads short a day and a 19,600 man-day shortfall over 175 working days, and 1,923 different people passed through roughly 1,024 seats in seven months with 906 exits, 47.1% attrition, a median tenure of two months and 73.8% leaving inside three months. Planning closed the picture: attainment ran 70.5% over May to July, 202,505 boxes planned against 142,866 actual, while the plant made 1.20 units for every unit shipped and stock rose 161% in a year.
levers: (1) Melting: eight high impact charging actions including off-line pre-sorting of entangled returns, charge mix staged on the platform ahead of the next heat, a second sampling die to split the 70 and 90 line loads, shot blasting of returns to cut slag, and a vibro feeder extension to remove the Furnace 5 charging delay; recipe and charge mix compliance brought under control to close the carbon and silicon corrections that drive the sampling loop. (2) Furnace reliability: ground leakage re-coded by physical failure path rather than by logged reason, so each unit falls into a contamination, refractory or electrical archetype and the programme is targeted at named units; coil cooling water control, water leakage closure, drain slopes and panel area protection installed against a dated action list. (3) Moulding line: cycle time variation control through operator training and SOP discipline, DISA moulding machine basic conditions restored on APC, hydraulics and lift table, punch out and transfer car brought into the same routine, and a preventive maintenance model that replaces one 24 hour weekly line shutdown with two focused 12 hour windows. (4) Core: a core supermarket with a minimum 45 minute buffer at the line, a WIP storage layout for both lines, trolley wheel and alignment reliability restored, SMED on the core feeding fixture changeover, and core planning taken off the manual register. (5) Sand plant: return sand group and mixer breakdown closure, pull cord protection, under conveyor bay lighting and wiring, and a source of contamination programme closing 33 named sand and dust ingress points on the D90 line. (6) Raw material: a future scrap yard layout with four zoned yards holding 5,030 MT at the standard mix, returns segregated at source for faster charging, and dead stock consumed to free the space. (7) Planning: a runner, repeater and stranger campaign model, 16 days, 6 days and 3 days a month, tested on 207 SKUs across a full year on the same demand, opening stock and receipts. (8) Manpower: contract fulfilment and attrition tracked at department and contractor level, with the four gated levers that convert available manpower into qualified capacity. (9) Governance: a steering committee routine with roughly 240 action points across ten workstreams, each with a named owner, a due date and a status, reviewed meeting to meeting.
impact: Diagnosis complete on both units across eleven workstreams and six gates in six weeks. Implementation live. Measured during the implementation window at the same production rate: metal delay on DF-70 down from 71 to 8 minutes a day, an 89% reduction, and on DF-90 from 61 to 26 minutes, a 58% reduction; core delay on DF-90 down from 43 to 23 minutes a day, a 46% reduction, and on DF-70 from 20 to 16 minutes; furnace first time right quality up by 2 points. The planning simulation showed on time dispatch fill moving from 97.4% to 98.0% and eventual fill to 100%, with closing backlog down 94%, gross production down 12%, average stock down 28% and closing stock down 45% on the same demand. The identified headroom is the gap between 458, 974 and 464 moulds a day and the 1,202, 2,083 and 1,200 the lines are rated for. No EBITDA figure is certified in the programme record. Do not quote one. Lead with the OEE decomposition, the delay reductions and the moulds a day gap, which are measured.
fit: Any iron or steel foundry, and any plant where a high pressure moulding line is the pacing asset: automotive and tractor castings, valve and pump bodies, pipe fittings, general jobbing foundries. The strongest analytical move is the finding that the moulding line is the bottleneck but does not own its own loss, because its output is capped by melt readiness, core availability and sand quality upstream of it. Use it with any foundry client whose reflex is to buy a faster line. Also the right case for a client who wants the loss shown in moulds a day rather than in percentages, and for a board that wants to see a diagnosis convert into a live action list with named owners inside weeks. Pairs with F5 the client and M18 the client for melt to casting throughput, with M26 the client for the constraint shift argument, and with P13 the client for the contract manpower fulfilment and attrition angle. Pitch angle: three lines, all below 50% OEE, and the largest single recoverable item was a 35 minute sampling loop against a 5 minute standard.

label: Steel and Alloy Castings Foundry
problem: The FY27 plan asks for ₹64 Cr of additional EBITDA on ₹128 Cr of additional sales, so the plan only closes if throughput, cost and quality move together. Throughput: the sand foundry has to go from 3,121 MT in the fourth quarter of FY26 to 4,000 MT a quarter, but the binding constraint is fettling rather than moulding. Fettling demand runs 1,110 MT a month in the first half and 1,335 MT in the second at 85% system efficiency, against a current 1,100 MT of combined in-house and vendor capacity, and the ecosystem study found more than 80 fettling shops with roughly 5,000 MT a month of capacity against 6,000 MT of demand, 67% of vendors under 100 MT, and vendor prices at ₹24 to ₹28 a kg against the ₹18 to ₹21 the plant currently pays. Quality: 388 customer complaints in FY26, of which 56% were found on machined castings, complaint PPM at 4,624 against a 500 target, and cost of poor quality at ₹25.4 Cr, of which ₹15.2 Cr is internal. The defect pareto is casting defects 156, dimensional 105 and thread 59, with sand inclusion, shell leak and gas porosity leading, most of them not detectable before machining, and 44% of parts going through rework after machining. Delivery: on time delivery at 51% overall, 53% for the top ten customers and 38% on new product development, against a 95% target, with inventory at 84 days. Cost: the FY26 to FY27 EBITDA bridge needs ₹25 Cr from cost reduction alone, with the sand system carrying most of it, weld electrode consumption at 22.6 kg a tonne against a target below 8, resin addition at 1.55%, and critical equipment availability at 80%.
levers: Short support to frame the initiative set rather than to run a programme. The initiatives identified sit in three places. Throughput: expand the Acero fettling facility from 300 to 600 MT, consolidate the vendor base to six or eight from a long tail, add capacity at named vendors to reach 1,400 MT a month by the first half, and lift foundry output through the 50T and 60T line changes. Cost: standardise on 100% new facing sand on the 50T line after the nine day trial, move the thermal to mechanical sand blend from 80:20 to 60:40 on non critical items, cut resin addition to 1.35%, and close the sand drying, bunker, catalyst pump and distribution constraints that the new sand recipe depends on. Quality: attack the defects that only appear after machining, through re-methoding, simulation and process validation, phased array ultrasonic testing to reduce radiography dependency, dimensional inspection on castings rather than only on machined parts, a complaint management process with a single register and owner, and a third party supplier quality audit routine across machining, fettling, heat treatment, painting and welding. Delivery: first in first out with heat code and year or week marking, a finished goods setup near the machine shop, a dedicated new product development cell, and part level lead time rules feeding the planning routine.
impact: Advisory support. No LFCC delivered result is certified in this record and no result should be attributed to LFCC. The value of the case is the diagnosis structure it demonstrates on a castings business: an EBITDA bridge decomposed into price, volume, cost reduction and opex, a throughput plan that identifies fettling rather than moulding as the constraint and sizes the regional vendor ecosystem against it, and a quality picture in which 56% of complaints are found after machining and cost of poor quality is more than a third of EBITDA. Present it as advisory work and as sector familiarity, not as a turnaround.
fit: Any steel, alloy or investment castings foundry, and any castings plus machining business supplying valve, pump, rail, mining or construction equipment OEMs. Use it when a board has approved a step change budget and wants the initiative set framed and sized before committing to a full programme, and when the client suspects the constraint is inside the plant but has not yet located it. The strongest move to reuse is the constraint test: the moulding lines can produce more, but fettling capacity, in-house and across the regional vendor base, sets what actually ships, and the ecosystem is fragmented enough that it has to be built rather than bought. Pairs with M28 the client, which is the implementation counterpart in the same industry, and with M26 the client for the same constraint shift logic in fabrication. Note on use: this is a short advisory engagement on a client owned plan, and parts of the client material carry third party marks, so do not present any of it as LFCC authored analysis or as a delivered case.

levers: Temperature/suction SOPs, BHS revamp, chemical efficiency trials, oxygen enrichment, PM adherence >90%, tiered MCS

label: Steel Integrated Mini Plant
problem: OEE 54% across Furnace–CCM–Rolling; heat cycle 118 min vs. 95 min; billet bypass 7–8%; no PM compliance

label: Refractories
problem: 447 deployed across 4 plants with no station-wise work plan. The studies found idle time and imbalance, not slow working. Pressing arms showed 17–33% output headroom at an 80% fatigue allowance. Kiln monitoring and reporting took 37–43% of the kiln team’s time. Kiln car pushers were idle 15–38% of the time during transfer-car moves. Casting crews of 7–8 worked every activity at random, with 4–19% idle. Maintenance ran at 46% utilisation on 8 heads. Skilled NSQF L5 stations ran on contract labour (FRP: 38 of 38 contract). Shape products are 70–78% of SR line items, which the plant team raised as a limit on scope.
levers: 4-tier method: (1) DILO and ratio-delay utilisation per person; (2) optimise where utilisation is below 80%, against standard deployment and SOP allocation; (3) impact analysis using past data for rare events, product variability and maintenance workload; (4) man-less machine research. Required manpower = frequency × standard time (observed average × PFD allowance) ÷ 8 shift hours. Levers: casting converted to a station-wise line (8→6 per team); final inspection and packing handover cut from 2 people to 1 after batch build-up; contractor packing paid per tonne; vibrating table for ramming; conveyor, pusher and flipper at tunnel-kiln cutting and grinding; automatic weigh-and-feed at the presses; laser profiler for 100% inline inspection; PLC kiln alarms and dashboards; electric tugger for kiln cars; integrated pallet strapping and wrapping, auto sieving and a liquid batching line at PACL. 3-phase action plan (no-cost, minor automation, major automation) with a named owner per action in Production, Maintenance, Projects, Purchase, Quality and IE.
impact: 447→320 (−127, 28.4%): SR-1 207→138 (−69, 33%); SR-2 165→127 (−38, 23%); PACL 32→23 (−9, 28%); FRP 43→32 (−11, 26%). 79 heads without automation, 48 with. Variability-adjusted scope agreed with the plant team: SR-1 28.2%, SR-2 19.6%. v11 carried 447→321 (−126) with PACL 32→24; corrected to the pack. The ₹4–6 Cr annual saving is not stated in the pack; treat it as indicative.
fit: Any specialty materials, refractories, ceramics or technical products manufacturer with a multi-plant workforce. Also any manufacturer where product variability is used as a reason to resist optimisation: the variability test answers the objection with data. Part of the the client group programme with P9, P14 and P15.

label: Abrasives — Manpower optimisation study

NSQF workforce mix: short term, 11 on-roll lead operators in IDC Spin and Sizer, belt on-roll raised from 2 to 6 at skiving and splicing, NSQF L3 certification for 50 of 74 flap-assembly contract workers; medium term, L5 maintenance (+12) and utility (+8) roles on-roll and 6 on-roll QC inspectors; end state 65–70% contract.

Labour saving ₹40.5 L a year at ₹2.70 L per person, so the labour-only payback is about 17.5 years overall (flexing conveyor 0.6 year, punching 3.9 years, spray and packing 8.2 years each); capacity and quality benefits are stated separately. fit: Any coated abrasives, converting or high-mix plant where the board expects a headcount cut. Strongest reference for a product-mix-adjusted fair benchmark, for automation ROI stated honestly on labour alone, and for contract-share risk on critical skill. Do not quote the v11 figures (Stage 1 405→356; 12 interventions at ₹40K–₹30L; ₹85 L–1 Cr, under 12-month payback; 25–35 additional FTE): none appears in the source pack (see v12 change log).

label: Tyre Manufacturer (Preparatory Section)

label: Electrical Equipment / Switchgear (RCCB)
problem: Contract share ranged from 51% to 76% and 86%, and each plant runs a different process. A single headcount target could not fit all 4 plants.
levers: One 4-step method at every plant: measure the work (DILO, ratio delay, VA / ENVA / NVA); grade it by skill (NSQF, 5 descriptors); size the levers by spend (no-spend redesign, then low-cost mechanisation, then capex with a payback case); test each number with the area team (product mix, rare events from past data, maintenance workload, area-owner review). Every head tested on 2 questions: volume (does the work need this person) and mix (is this person on the right terms for the skill). The releasable time fell into 3 recurring patterns: waiting on machine cycles, manual transfer between stations, and tending legacy manual machines.

Productive time at 10 studied stations was 23–55% of the shift. Indicative value at contract rates (₹2.4–2.7 L per head a year) is about ₹9–10 Cr a year; not stated in any pack, do not quote as a finding.
fit: Any multi-plant group, especially where plants differ in process and labour mix. An integrated case-study deck was built in September 2026 for the the client leadership team. Figures are study findings, not realised savings, and must be framed that way.

label: Abrasives — Manpower Optimisation
problem: Slack at the presses and in finishing. 400T/600T presses ran 33–44% utilised, with 4+ hours of break and 2+ hours idle a shift. The big presses lost 25–40% of the shift to breaks and 19–24% to waiting for mix. Mixing flexi ran at 49–56%, bore painting at 32–37%, and the shaving machines at 30–36% with 43–46% idle. Legacy manual machines tied operators down: a ~40-year-old edger needed 2 people; shaving took 10:47 per piece by hand; a diamond-discing operator watched a 25-minute cut in a 32-minute cycle. Permanent share was 49% of 403 graded heads against a ~30% skill-demand benchmark, and the NSQF L4 band ran 62% permanent. Intra-shift idle: NMS about 0 vs flexi 20–60 minutes.
levers: Lever 1, volume: line balancing and multi-machine manning on Module 2 (21 of 25 machines automatic or semi-automatic; 19 heads, no capex); layout redesign of Module 3 (NMS 10 + flexi 6 → NMS 7 + flexi 3) and Module 4; PLC and servo retrofit of shaving, GKW disc, diamond disc and balancing machines (₹39–56 L, 6 operators, ₹26.5 L a year, 21-month payback, 3-year NPV +₹18.9 L at 10%; 85–90% capital saving against ₹3.2–4.8 Cr for new CNCs); auto weighing, dispensing and levelling at the 1,500T, 1,000T and RCT presses; auto-strapping and palletising. Lever 2, mix: over-graded L2–L4 permanent roles re-graded over 18 months through attrition and redeployment, with no retrenchment; 18 experienced operators become setter-leads (setting, first-off and quality across a machine cluster); presses, mixing, kiln and skilled L5–L6 work stay permanent with 1 cross-trained backup each. Attendance design for piece-rate work: attendance bonus, guaranteed base plus output slabs, gang piece-rate, full-shift quota for the top rate, quality-gated payment, binding roster; about 15% flexible cover buffer.
impact: 483→415 (−68, 14%): 44 without automation, 24 with. Module 1 −7 (13%), Module 2 −19 (10%), Module 3 −12 (17%), Module 4 −24 (18%), Module 3b −2 (11%), Engineering −4 (16%). Labour productivity +16% (same output from 415); throughput +7–25% in areas kept; cycle time −46% on automated lines (shaving 10:47→5:51 per piece); 30–40% energy saving on retrofitted drives. Mix: permanent 197→139 of 403 graded heads (49%→35%); 58 roles re-graded, 18 retained as setter-leads. The pack gives two conflicting people-cost values (₹1.3–1.5 Cr and ₹1.8 Cr); do not quote a rupee figure.
fit: Any bonded abrasives, grinding wheel, press-and-fire or resin-bonded products plant; any plant with legacy manual machines where retrofit beats replacement; any plant with a high permanent share on routine work. For external audiences, keep the mix lever at the level of percentages and principles; do not quote re-grade counts.

label: Technical Ceramics
problem: Paired machines each carried their own operator well below capacity: SACMI team member at 23% VA; Ball Press 1 at 24% and C14 at 40% utilisation; ISO press trainees at 33–36% through an 18-minute cycle; palletiser VA 27%; Wear Resistant Line moulding at 44.1% average machine utilisation. Manual transfer: the alumina cleaning helper spent 41% of the shift on trolley transfer. Machine-wait: the WPS fine-grinding helper waited 37% of the study. An installed robot on EP5 and EP6 was not running, so stacking had reverted to manual. Lined Equipment: 13 DILO studies over 3,372 observed minutes showed 862 minutes (26%) of pure NVA, with idle waiting the largest loss.
levers: Priority 1, Just-Do-It (0–6 weeks): rebalancing, standard work, multi-machine manning, helper pooling and roster levelling (SACMI + Ball Press-3 9→6; BP1 + C14 6→3; Fired Ware 32→26 through scrubber cleaning and one packer per 2 lines; Lined Equipment lining −12, painting −7). Priority 3, capex (4–12 months, after cycle-time validation, specification and a payback case): robot-assisted DBP/VTC conveyor cell (6→3 per shift), SACMI robotic pick and place, ECT semi-auto loading with automatic pass/fail sort (18→9), glaze spray robot cell with ultrasonic mask cleaning (4→2), automated inline drying after nickel plating, robots on EP1/EP2 and EP8/EP3, automated box packing.
impact: 982→826 (−156, 16%): Engineering Ceramics −25 (18%), MC Line 1 −47 (22%), MC Line 2 −24 (16%), Wear Resistant Line −33 (17%), Lined Equipment −27 (27%). 78 Just-Do-It (50%), 36 low-cost, 42 capex. Quality, Maintenance, RBC and CMP 1–2 were studied and no reduction was proposed.
fit: Any technical ceramics, engineered components, wear-resistant products or lined-equipment plant; any plant with paired machines under 40% utilisation or installed automation that has stopped running. The strongest spend-tiered case in the library: lead with ‘half the scope needs no spend’.

label: Electrical Components (terminal blocks, moulding, sheet metal)
sector: Electrical Components (terminal blocks, moulding, sheet metal)
problem: Idle time sat in specific roles, not across the plant. Sheet metal sub-roles ran 14–51% idle (Bihler line leader 38% VA, 51% idle; YSM operator 44% VA, 41% idle; ultrasonic 41% VA, 42% idle). impact: 684→628 (−56, 8.2%); ₹13.44 L a month, ₹1.61 Cr a year gross; one-time transition cost ₹3–5 L; net year-1 about ₹156 L. Sheet Metal −8 (7%), IJM-D7 −15 (12%), IJM-B101 −11 (20%), Auto Assembly −1 (1%), Dispatch −21 (29%). label: Electrical Controls
problem: Supervisory and staff headcount was expected to rise in step with a 20% annual volume plan, with no measure of how supervisors spent their time or how much of it was value-added.
levers: 4-step method: (1) manpower load and estimation: org-structure mapping; DILO with readings every 2–3 minutes; classification into VA, NVA, rework and meeting idle; classification reviewed with stakeholders and managers; (2) historical growth: 5 years of items inward, items issued, production changeovers, machine hours and utilisation; (3) process critique: daily workload change and expected man-hours at the higher load; (4) a capacity and resource estimator for growth. Each KRA split into regular and periodic activity, breaks removed, and VA minutes needed per KRA summed per post. Activities flagged for removal once an OPEX supervisor is appointed or a planning module goes live (material searching, transfer-order generation, posting rework, SCN meeting time).

The pack does not state a final supervisor or manager headcount, and the Store, SFG, Planning, Purchase and Logistics results are not in it: do not quote a headcount.

The forward-build anchor: size supervisory need from measured VA per KRA before hiring for growth. Pairs with P13 the client (deployment discipline) and P16 the client (restraint). label: Cement (Saudi Arabia) — Manufacturing Assessment (2)
problem: Kiln MTBF running 7× below international benchmark. HFO (Heavy Fuel Oil) utilisation below optimal. White cement SPC above benchmark. SHC above benchmark by 100–200 kcal/kg.
levers: Kiln reliability analysis (MTBF gap quantified vs. benchmark). HFO utilisation optimisation. White cement SPC reduction levers. SHC reduction programme (100–200 kcal/kg target). Zero-CapEx levers identified separately.
impact: SAR 16–26.5 Mn total; SAR 16 Mn zero-CapEx component. MTBF improvement, SPC white cement −15%, SHC −100–200 kcal/kg.
fit: Any cement manufacturer with kiln reliability and energy cost issues, particularly white cement producers. MTBF 7× below benchmark is a powerful opening hook — it signals reactive maintenance culture in a capital-intensive process.

label: Cement (Saudi Arabia) — Detailed Operational Diagnosis
problem: Across the line, equipment reliability is world-class but calendar availability is not — and the root of it sits in the Raw Mill. Kiln-01 net OEE is 86.4% (net availability 98.4%, breakdowns just 0.9% of lost time) yet gross calendar OEE is only 49% (availability 55.8%, performance 87.8%, quality 100%). Raw Mill-01 mirrors it: net OEE 85.0% but gross OEE 44.9%; breakdowns only 2.5% of calendar time, while planned shutdowns (27%) and circumstantial feed/fuel stoppages (20%) consume the rest. The binding constraint is Raw Mill availability: Raw Mill uptime 90.4% versus kiln 98.8%, stopping roughly every 2.5 days (16 stops in a 45-day window), each stop cutting kiln feed ~25% for ~6.5 hours. Three failure modes drive 62% of Raw Mill incident downtime — hydraulic faults, limestone weigh-feeder trips, rotary-feeder trips — with zero RCA completed across all ten root causes. The cross-equipment mechanism is the key finding: a Raw Mill stop diverts hot gas to the bag house, recirculates dust, lifts raw-meal LSF and free-lime tendency, so operators cut kiln feed to protect quality — lowering clinker output at near-constant heat input and pushing SHC up. Kiln daily output averages 5,341 TPD against a 6,300 target (−15%), hitting target on just 2 of 211 producing days, with a sharp seasonal collapse to 18% availability in Jun/Jul/Dec versus 69% elsewhere. Energy gaps compound it: SHC 805 kcal/kg vs 770 target; Cement Mill-2 SPC 45.9 kWh/t vs own best-ever 30.9; Raw Mill specific power falls ~10% simply by loading toward design feed, with mill-inlet gas temperature and bang-bang dampers as further levers. Maintenance effectiveness is weak despite 100% PM compliance: 1,097 abnormalities over 9 months, 559 open, 71% high priority, 52% blocked on spares, 49% air-leakage-related, 86% of CM2 failures repeat modes. Instrumentation down: O₂/CO analysers offline >1.5 years, auto-sampler dead 2–3 years, kiln/clinker sampling compliance 48%. Plant 5S maturity 20% vs 80% benchmark. The cement mill tells the same story: Cement Mill-2 net OEE is 83.4% when running but only 24.1% on a calendar basis, with 94% of its downtime silo-full or planned rather than breakdowns, and ~15% mill rejection (37.8 t/h) driven by operating state — outlet gas temperature, circulation-fan damper, feed rate — not clinker chemistry.
levers: Five-lever action plan, 54 actions (13 one-time, 32 systemic, 9 periodic), anchored by a Raw Mill reliability programme. (1) Raw Mill reliability + HFO banking — RCA-led fix of the top-three failure modes to lift MTBF from ~2.5 to ≥5 days, a seasonal failure-prevention plan ahead of Jun/Jul/Dec, plus ~60-day HFO banking to run 75+ day kiln campaigns and cut stops from ~28 to 2–3/year. (2) Throughput discipline — sustain ≥6,000 TPD then stretch to 6,300 TPD, real-time kiln-feed monitoring with alerts below 380 t/h, SIC on Roller Press/Kiln/Cement Mill, LSF variability reduction at raw mill. (3) Power/SPC reduction — load the raw mill toward design feed (~10% specific-power gain at no capital cost), modulating damper and mill-inlet-gas control, EMS + daily equipment-level metering, RP-1/RP-2 meter separation, restore best-month grinding SPC (CM2 −32.7%), and curb the ~15% cement-mill rejection by cutting cold starts (startup rejection runs ~28% above steady-state) and holding the validated 70–79% circulation-damper window. (4) SHC reduction — recover the ~91 Raw-Mill-off hours that occur while the kiln runs, false-air closure, cooler-fan re-balance, refractory cycle discipline, restore pyrometer and gas analysers, hourly sampling. (5) Reliability governance — abnormality classification and closure with an RCA culture replacing PM-compliance theatre, FMEA, monthly heat-balance audits, 5S rollout, and a daily/weekly/monthly performance-dialogue cadence. Three deep RCAs delivered in-diagnosis (boiler trip, deep-pan conveyor, C5 cyclone choking traced to kiln-feed chloride 0.117% vs 0.020%).
impact: SAR 6 Mn/year identified on the client alone, phased across a 6-month implementation roadmap (Jul–Dec 2026, two kiln campaigns). Target KPIs: SHC 805→770 kcal/kg (−4.3%); SPC 93.9→81.6 kWh/t (−13.1%); throughput 228→260 TPH and 5,480→6,300 TPD (+14%); availability 56→59%. Raw Mill reliability lever alone recovers ~65 TPD daily average and, by holding kiln feed above 420 t/h, pulls SHC from ~850 toward ~777 kcal/kg. Energy 7.1 Mn kWh/year (SAR 1.61 Mn/year recurring); combined SHC+SPC cement value up to SAR 4.7 Mn; 52,401 ton/year additional clinker from HFO saved. Diagnosis stage — implementation roadmap delivered and sequenced; closeout numbers to follow the programme tracker.
fit: Any cement manufacturer where the binding constraint is upstream reliability and fuel security rather than equipment failure — the “your kiln is world-class, but a raw mill that stops every 2.5 days is starving it and inflating your heat rate” story. Strongest reference in the library for two distinct analytical moves: separating net OEE (world-class) from gross calendar availability (~45–49%) to reframe where the money sits, and tracing a downstream symptom (high kiln SHC, low clinker output) to an upstream cause (raw mill stoppages forcing kiln-feed cuts). Deepest cement diagnosis LFC has produced. Pairs with C1 (the client) and C2: C2 is the both-lines opportunity-identification assessment; C3 is the the client implementation-ready diagnosis that converts it. Lead with C3 when the prospect wants implementation depth and a cross-equipment loss-tree, not just an opportunity number.

label: Cement (India) — Maintenance & Reliability
problem: Preventive, predictive and breakdown maintenance running side by side with no strategy separating them. Reactive intervention on the three installations that decide cement output: gear boxes, mills and the kiln.
levers: Maintenance practice rebuilt around critical installations. Condition-based monitoring on kiln temperature, pressure and vibration. Equipment-specific schedules replacing generic templates. Performance threshold-based maintenance triggers. Tiered line walks to flag abnormalities. Automated MTTR and MTBF tracking, downtime trend analysis, and reporting of primary issue sources.
impact: Uptime +16%; OEE 92%; maintenance cost −20%; MTTR −68%; MTBF +16%; scheduled maintenance compliance 100%; raw mill uptime 95%; finish mill uptime 95%; maintenance activity completion 100%.
fit: Any cement manufacturer where maintenance is executed to schedule but failure modes are not being eliminated, or where reliability metrics are improving without releasing availability. Strongest India cement reference for equipment reliability and maintenance strategy.

label: Cement (India) — Process, Energy & Quality
scale: Large multi-site Indian cement and RMC group
problem: Clinker output and clinker quality both constrained by three interacting inputs: raw material quality, coal quality and kiln temperature distribution. Coal energy capacity, coal moisture content and coal cost all moving without control. Recipe adherence and testing adherence below the level the product mix required.
levers: Quality systems and feed-rate control brought under one programme rather than sequenced. Automated tracking of raw material feed rate. Process parameter variation tracking. Periodic production performance monitoring. Grade-wise recipe adherence tracking. Scheduled raw material, coal and ground cement sampling with QC adherence monitoring. Shopfloor CLIT/CLRI checklists at operator level. Coal quality parameter testing scheduled and monitored.
impact: Throughput +15%; energy cost −11%; coal consumption −7%; capacity utilisation 91%; recipe adherence 98%; quality adherence 96%; cement cost −6%; raw material and ground cement testing adherence 100%.
fit: Any cement manufacturer with energy cost pressure where the diagnosis is likely to land on input variability and process stability rather than on equipment. The throughput gain and the energy gain came from the same work, which is the argument for treating them as one programme. Largest India cement reference by client scale.

label: Cement (India) — Logistics & Dispatch
problem: Finished goods inventory and fill rate moving against each other. Push replenishment, unconnected production planning, non-moving stock accumulating, and fleet cost carried without utilisation discipline. Cement made and not moved is not sold.
levers: Pull-based finished goods inventory management. FG replenishment model tracking inventory level and ageing. Production planning connected to dispatch. On-time dispatch adherence monitoring. Vehicle arrangement scheduling and compliance monitoring. Optimal vehicle selection for load utilisation. Vehicle loading monitoring to cut idle time. Fleet maintenance management to cut vehicle downtime. Non-moving stock monitoring.
impact: OTIF +30%; non-moving stock value −25%; fleet utilisation +14%; fill rate 96%; vehicle load utilisation 94%; vehicle downtime +17%; vehicle idle time +9%; logistics cost per MT −3%; inventory cost −2%.
fit: Any cement producer, or any bulk building-materials manufacturer, where the plant is not the constraint and the dispatch chain is. Also the right case where inventory and fill rate are being traded against each other. Only India cement case in the library on logistics rather than process.
